interactions.label: Which combination of features correctly identifies cardiac muscle on histologica

params.question: Which combination of features correctly identifies cardiac muscle on histological examination?

answers.text: Long cylindrical fibres with peripheral nuclei and visible striations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features describe skeletal muscle — the voluntary, striated type attached to bones. Its nuclei are characteristically pushed to the periphery of the fibre.

answers.text: Short branched fibres with central nuclei, striations, and intercalated discs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cardiac muscle is uniquely identified by its short branched fibres, centrally placed nuclei, visible striations, and intercalated discs that coordinate the heart's rhythmic contraction.

answers.text: Spindle-shaped cells with central nuclei and no visible striations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features identify smooth muscle — the non-striated involuntary type found in hollow organs such as the intestine, blood vessels, and uterus.

answers.text: Branched fibres with peripheral nuclei and intercalated discs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cardiac muscle does have branched fibres and intercalated discs, but its nuclei are centrally placed, not peripheral. Peripheral nuclei are the hallmark of skeletal muscle.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cardiac muscle has short branched fibres, central nuclei, striations, and intercalated discs. Remember: peripheral nuclei → skeletal; central nuclei + no striations → smooth; central nuclei + striations + intercalated discs → cardiac.
Well done! The S-V-P rule helps remember skeletal muscle: Striated + Voluntary + Peripheral nuclei. Cardiac muscle shares striations but is involuntary with central nuclei and intercalated discs.

params.question: A pathologist examining a muscle biopsy observes a connective tissue layer wrapping individual muscle fibres, with capillaries and nerve terminals in direct contact. Which layer is this?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The epimysium is the outermost dense connective tissue coat surrounding the entire muscle, not individual fibres.
The perimysium wraps fascicles — bundles of fibres — and carries blood vessels and nerves towards them, but it does not directly contact individual fibres.

Correct. The endomysium is the innermost connective tissue layer, wrapping each individual muscle fibre. This is where capillaries and nerve terminals make direct contact, enabling fibre nutrition and motor control.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of the muscle fibre itself. It lies beneath the endomysium and is not classified as a connective tissue layer.

overallFeedback.feedback: The endomysium wraps each individual fibre and is where capillaries and nerve endings establish direct contact. Think: epi- = upon the whole muscle, peri- = around the fascicle bundle, endo- = within, around the single fibre.

Correct! Remember the hierarchy from outside in: epimysium (whole muscle) → perimysium (fascicle) → endomysium (individual fibre). The Greek prefixes are the key — epi (upon), peri (around), endo (within).

interactions.label: When catching a fast-moving ball, which muscle becomes proportionally more activ

params.question: When catching a fast-moving ball, which muscle becomes proportionally more active at the elbow to prevent the joint surfaces from separating?

answers.text: Brachialis — because it is the deep flexor of the elbow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The brachialis is a spurt muscle. Its line of pull passes mostly across the bone, producing large angular movement at the joint, not compression of the articular surfaces.

answers.text: Biceps brachii — because its two heads generate maximum force

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The biceps brachii is also a spurt muscle. Despite its power, its dominant force component is rotary — creating angular movement rather than stabilising the joint.

answers.text: Brachioradialis — because its pull runs along the bone, compressing the joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The brachioradialis is the classic shunt muscle at the elbow. Its line of pull runs mostly along the radius, generating a stabilising force that compresses the articular surfaces together and prevents joint separation.

answers.text: Pronator teres — because it crosses both the elbow and radioulnar joints

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pronator teres primarily pronates the forearm. It was not described in MacConaill's classification as a shunt muscle at the elbow.

overallFeedback.feedback: The brachioradialis is the key shunt muscle at the elbow. Shunt muscles pull along the bone to compress and stabilise the joint; spurt muscles (brachialis, biceps) pull across the bone to create angular movement. Both types always work together.

Well done! Spurt muscles (brachialis, biceps) create the angular movement, while the shunt muscle (brachioradialis) simultaneously guards the joint against separation — especially critical during rapid movements like catching.
